exp1.title: Experiment 1: belief networks on the effects of AI on learners' thinking and learning
about: Two sets of six news articles on the effects of AI on learners: a balanced set and a set of negatively charged articles, chosen by a written rule from nineteen labelled articles.

For each set, Claude Sonnet 5.5 generated statements ten times in each of two ways (the beliefs a reader could form from the articles, and the propositions the articles contain) and three times as statements about the articles as texts. Claude Opus 5.5 generated one reference list per set.

Sonnet split compound statements, and Opus checked the splits. Sonnet proposed matching statements across runs, and Opus accepted or rejected each proposed pair; the forty statements that recurred most formed the list.
Claude Haiku 4.5 was then prompted for ratings of the forty statements and their negations, and for the related pairs among them. These later steps are folded below.

steps.label: Reader beliefs from six articles
steps.asks: List the beliefs about the world that a reader of these articles could come to hold after reading them.

template.name: gen_reader_beliefs.txt
template.text:
Here are {n_articles} news articles on one topic, labelled {labels}. The names of the outlets have been removed.

{articles}

Task: list the beliefs about the world that a reader of these articles could come to hold after reading them.

A belief here is a statement about the world that a reader could accept or reject: about what happened or is the case, what a number is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each belief is one declarative statement with exactly one claim. Test every belief before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which a reader could accept while rejecting the other, divide it and list both. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal belief (A causes B) is one statement only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each belief must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the articles must be able to understand it. Give full names, and include the time, place and population when the statement's truth depends on them.
3. State the belief about the world, not about the articles or about what someone said: write the claim itself, not that a person or study made it.
4. Include beliefs that one article supports and another disputes, beliefs that several articles bear on together, and beliefs that a reader could take away although no single sentence states them. Every belief must be one that these articles bear on; do not add beliefs the articles do not touch.
5. Write each belief so that a person could agree or disagree with it. Do not hedge it with "may" or "might" unless the uncertainty is the claim.
6. List {n} beliefs. Do not list the same belief twice in different words.

For each belief, list the articles that bear on it and how: "supports" (a reader of that article would be led toward the belief), "disputes" (led away from it), or "mixed" (the article gives evidence both ways).

Return JSON of the form {{"beliefs": [{{"text": "<belief>", "articles": [{{"article": "<label>", "bearing": "supports|disputes|mixed"}}]}}, ...]}}.

steps.label: Propositions from six articles
steps.asks: List the propositions about the world that these articles contain.

template.name: gen_propositions.txt
template.text:
Here are {n_articles} news articles on one topic, labelled {labels}. The names of the outlets have been removed.

{articles}

Task: list the propositions about the world that these articles contain.

A proposition is a single claim about the world that an article states or reports: what happened or is the case, what a number is, what a rule or status is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each proposition contains exactly one claim. Test every proposition before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, or a fact and a comment on it are two claims. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal claim (A causes B) is one proposition only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each proposition must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the articles must be able to understand it. Resolve pronouns, give full names, and include the time, place and population when the claim's truth depends on them. Add nothing else.
3. State the proposition as a claim about the world, not about the article. When an article reports a claim made by a person or a study, state the claim itself and record the source in "relation" and "source"; do not write "the article says".
4. Keep the article's meaning. Do not strengthen, weaken, generalise or soften the claim.
5. Leave out rhetorical flourishes, questions, and claims whose meaning cannot be resolved from the article.
6. Each proposition must come from the articles. Give the article label and copy, character for character, the shortest passage of that article that states it ("span"). If several articles state the same proposition, list it once and give every article that states it.
7. List {n} propositions, chosen to cover what the articles say, including the claims on which they disagree. Do not list the same proposition twice in different words.

For each article that states the proposition, give "relation": "asserts" (the article states it in its own voice), "reports" (the article reports a person, group or study saying it), or "hedges" (the article states it with doubt or qualification), and "source": who makes the claim (a person, group or study as named in the article, or "the article" when it is the article's own voice).

Return JSON of the form {{"propositions": [{{"text": "<proposition>", "evidence": [{{"article": "<label>", "span": "<exact passage>", "relation": "asserts|reports|hedges", "source": "<who>"}}]}}, ...]}}.

steps.label: Statements about the articles as texts
steps.asks: List statements that describe these articles as texts, rather than the world they report on.

template.name: gen_analysis.txt
template.text:
Here are {n_articles} news articles on one topic, labelled {labels}. The names of the outlets have been removed.

{articles}

Task: list statements that describe these articles as texts, rather than the world they report on. There are three kinds.
- "text": a statement about one article as a piece of writing: its tone, what it emphasises or leaves out, whose views it gives most space to, whether its headline claims more or less than its body.
- "entity": a statement about how one article represents a person, group or institution: favourably or unfavourably, as credible or not, as acting from a given motive.
- "between": a statement about how two or more of the articles relate: that they agree or disagree on a point, that one reports a study the other omits, that they frame the same finding differently.

Rules: each statement makes exactly one claim (if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both; do not join two claims with "and", "while", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon); it names the article or articles by label (for example "Article A2"); it can be checked by reading the articles; it does not say whether the article is right about the world. List {n} statements, with each kind represented. Do not list the same statement twice in different words.

Return JSON of the form {{"statements": [{{"text": "<statement>", "kind": "text|entity|between", "articles": ["<label>", ...]}}, ...]}}.

steps.label: Splitting compound statements
steps.asks: Split every statement that makes more than one claim into statements that each make exactly one claim.

template.name: split.txt
template.text:
Here are {n} statements.

{statements}

Task: split every statement that makes more than one claim into statements that each make exactly one claim.

A statement makes more than one claim when it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, a claim and the reason or explanation given for it, a fact and a comment on it, and two prescriptions are each two claims. A causal statement (A causes B) is one claim when the causal link is the claim. "And" inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about, does not make two claims.

Rules for the parts.
1. Each part makes exactly one claim.
2. Taken together, the parts say what the original said: nothing added, nothing dropped, nothing strengthened or weakened.
3. Each part stands on its own: repeat the subject, time, place and population in every part where the claim's truth depends on them, and resolve pronouns.
4. Use the original's words as far as possible.
5. A statement that already makes one claim is returned unchanged, as a list with that one statement, copied exactly.

Return JSON of the form {{"split": {{"b0": ["<part>", "<part>"], "b1": ["<statement unchanged>"], ...}}}} with every statement id.

steps.label: Checking the splits
steps.asks: For each statement, answer two questions. 1. "together": do the parts, taken together, say what the original said?

template.name: split_check.txt
template.text:
Here are {n} statements, each split into parts.

{items}

For each statement, answer two questions.
1. "together": do the parts, taken together, say what the original said? "yes" (nothing added, dropped, strengthened or weakened), "partly" (close, but something is added, dropped or changed), or "no".
2. "single": for each part, in order, does it make exactly one claim, that is, can it not be divided into two statements each of which could be true while the other is false? A list of "yes" or "no", one per part.
Judge meaning only; do not judge whether any statement is true.

Return JSON of the form {{"checks": {{"s0": {{"together": "yes|partly|no", "single": ["yes", ...]}}, ...}}}} with every id.

steps.label: Matching statements across runs
steps.asks: Find every pair (one statement from List X, one from List Y) that states the same proposition.

template.name: judge_same.txt
template.text:
Here are two lists of statements.

List X:
{list_x}

List Y:
{list_y}

Task: find every pair (one statement from List X, one from List Y) that states the same proposition.

Rule. Two statements state the same proposition when each entails the other: anyone who accepts the first must accept the second, and anyone who accepts the second must accept the first, given ordinary background knowledge and nothing else. Wording, word order and level of detail in phrasing do not matter; meaning does. They are not the same proposition when one is more specific than the other (a different time, place, population, quantity or degree), when one contains a claim the other lacks, when one is a cause and the other only an association, when one attributes the claim to a source and the other does not, or when they are about the same topic but claim different things. A statement and its negation are never the same proposition.

Consider every pair. A statement may match more than one statement in the other list. For each matching pair, give a one-sentence reason.

Return JSON of the form {{"same": [{{"x": "<id from List X>", "y": "<id from List Y>", "reason": "..."}}, ...]}}. Return {{"same": []}} if no pair matches.

steps.label: Judging the proposed matches
steps.asks: For each pair, say how statement A relates to statement B in meaning. Choose one relation: - "same": each entails the other (anyone who accepts one must accept the other). - "a_implies_b":

template.name: judge_relation.txt
template.text:
Here are {n} pairs of statements.

{pairs}

For each pair, say how statement A relates to statement B in meaning. Choose one relation:
- "same": each entails the other (anyone who accepts one must accept the other).
- "a_implies_b": A entails B, but B does not entail A.
- "b_implies_a": B entails A, but A does not entail B.
- "contradiction": exactly one of them is true in every case (one is the negation of the other).
- "contrary": they cannot both be true, but they can both be false.
- "related": neither entails the other and they are compatible, but they are about the same matter.
- "unrelated": they are about different matters.
Judge meaning only, given ordinary background knowledge; do not judge whether either statement is true.

Return JSON of the form {{"relations": {{"p0": "<relation>", "p1": "<relation>", ...}}}} with every pair id.

steps.label: Typing each statement
steps.asks: For each statement, give two labels.

template.name: type_statements.txt
template.text:
Here are {n} statements.

{statements}

For each statement, give two labels.

"about": what the statement is about.
- "world": the world itself (events, quantities, causes, rules, what should be done).
- "text": an article as a piece of writing (its tone, emphasis, headline, what it includes or omits).
- "entity": how an article represents a person, group or institution.
- "between": how two or more articles relate to each other.

"content": what kind of claim it is.
- "event_state": factual; that something happened or is the case.
- "quantity": factual; a number, share, size or change in amount.
- "rule_status": factual; a law, policy, rule, official decision or formal status.
- "characterising": interpretive; describes the nature or character of something in terms that involve judgement.
- "causal": interpretive; that one thing causes, affects or explains another.
- "predictive": interpretive; what will or is likely to happen.
- "moral": evaluative; that something is good, bad, right, wrong, fair or unfair.
- "prescriptive": evaluative; what should or should not be done.
A factual claim can in principle be settled by evidence; an interpretive claim needs judgement beyond the evidence; an evaluative claim depends on values. Choose the single label that fits the main claim. Judge only the kind of claim, not whether it is true.

Return JSON of the form {{"labels": {{"b0": {{"about": "...", "content": "..."}}, ...}}}} with every statement id.

steps.label: Writing negations and paraphrases
steps.asks: For each statement, write five related statements. 1. "negation": the statement's contradiction.

template.name: derive.txt
template.text:
Here are {n} statements.

{statements}

For each statement, write five related statements.
1. "negation": the statement's contradiction. It must be true exactly when the original is false. Negate the main claim and nothing else; prefer a natural wording ("does not lower", "is not the main cause") to an opposite ("raises", "is a minor cause"), because an opposite is a contrary, not a contradiction. Do not use a double negation.
2. "weaker": a slightly weaker version: one that the original implies but that does not imply the original (for example narrower in scope, less extreme, or less certain in degree), otherwise as close to the original as possible.
3. "stronger": a slightly stronger version: one that implies the original but is not implied by it, otherwise as close to the original as possible.
4. "paraphrase_1" and "paraphrase_2": two rewordings with exactly the same meaning as the original, worded differently from it and from each other.
5. "negation_paraphrase_1" and "negation_paraphrase_2": two rewordings with exactly the same meaning as your negation.

Every statement you write must stand on its own and keep the time, place and population of the original.

Return JSON of the form {{"derived": {{"b0": {{"negation": "...", "weaker": "...", "stronger": "...", "paraphrase_1": "...", "paraphrase_2": "...", "negation_paraphrase_1": "...", "negation_paraphrase_2": "..."}}, ...}}}} with every statement id.

steps.label: Checking propositions against their article
steps.asks: For each proposition, answer three questions about this article only. 1. "supported": does the article, read as a whole, state or report the proposition with the same meaning?

template.name: faithfulness.txt
template.text:
Here is a news article, labelled {label}.

{article}

Here are {n} propositions, each with a passage said to come from this article and a description of how the article states it.

{items}

For each proposition, answer three questions about this article only.
1. "supported": does the article, read as a whole, state or report the proposition with the same meaning? "yes", "partly" (the article states something close but the proposition adds, drops or changes part of the meaning), or "no".
2. "relation_correct": is the description of how the article states it ("asserts" in its own voice, "reports" a source saying it, "hedges") correct? "yes" or "no".
3. "standalone": can the proposition be understood correctly without the article? "yes" or "no".
Judge against the article, not against your own knowledge of the world.

Return JSON of the form {{"checks": {{"q0": {{"supported": "...", "relation_correct": "...", "standalone": "..."}}, ...}}}} with every id.

steps.label: Checking reader beliefs against the articles
steps.asks: For each statement, answer two questions about this article only. 1. "bearing": does this article bear on the statement?

template.name: faithfulness_reader.txt
template.text:
Here is a news article, labelled {label}.

{article}

Here are propositions taken from this article, each with the passage it was taken from checked by program against the article.

{propositions}

Here are {n} statements about the world that a reader of several articles, this one among them, might come to hold.

{statements}

For each statement, answer two questions about this article only.
1. "bearing": does this article bear on the statement? "supports" (a reader of this article would be led toward the statement), "opposes" (led away from it), "addresses" (the article addresses the matter without leading either way), or "none" (the article does not address it).
2. "propositions": if the article bears on the statement, the ids of the propositions above that carry that bearing, or an empty list if the bearing does not rest on any of them.
Judge against the article, not against your own knowledge of the world.

Return JSON of the form {{"checks": {{"b0": {{"bearing": "supports|opposes|addresses|none", "propositions": ["q0", ...]}}, ...}}}} with every statement id.

gen3.title: Beliefs generated for five more topics
gen3.question: Can the models under test generate the belief set from the articles, following the ontology, with checks strict enough to make the set rigorous?
about: The procedure of an earlier run (“Beliefs generated by the models”, 29 September), applied to five more topics: tariffs and prices, congestion pricing, GLP-1 drugs, AI and learning, and nuclear revival.
For each topic, ten news articles in date order, each cut to its first 260 words.
Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5, through the Claude Code command line, each generated claims of one type per request (factual, interpretive or evaluative), four times.
GPT-5.4 mini checked each claim’s kind, form and neutrality, and whether it is faithful to its article. Sonnet 5 grouped the claims that say the same thing.
Through the command line, Claude Code’s own system prompt comes first and the study’s system prompt is appended.

steps.label: Claims from ten articles, one type per request
steps.group: Writing, checking and grouping the claims
steps.asks: List claims about the subject of these articles that a reader could believe or disbelieve.

steps.label: Checking each claim's kind, form and neutrality
steps.group: Writing, checking and grouping the claims
steps.asks: Classify each of the following claims.

steps.label: Checking each claim against its article
steps.group: Writing, checking and grouping the claims
steps.asks: Check each claim below against these articles. For a claim marked [factual], answer faithful = true only if at least one article states or clearly implies the claim as it is worded, with no detail added or changed.

steps.label: Grouping claims that say the same thing
steps.group: Writing, checking and grouping the claims
steps.asks: Group together claims that state the same proposition with the same polarity, so that anyone who agrees with one would agree with the others. Claims that are merely related, or that disagree, go in different groups.

template.name: props_A.txt
template.text:
The following news article is labelled {labels}. The name of the outlet has been removed.

{articles}

Task: list the propositions about the world that the article labelled {target} contains.

A proposition is a single claim about the world that an article states or reports: what happened or is the case, what a number is, what a rule or status is, what causes what, what will happen, or what is good, bad or should be done. Follow these rules.
1. Each proposition contains exactly one claim. Test every proposition before you list it: if it can be divided into two statements, each of which could be true while the other is false, divide it and list both. Two numbers, two findings, a finding and a second finding about its size or timing, or a fact and a comment on it are two claims. Do not join two claims with "and", "while", "with", "as well as", "but", "which", a comma or a semicolon. "And" may appear only inside a name, or in a list that is itself the single thing the claim is about. A causal claim (A causes B) is one proposition only when the causal link is the claim.
2. Each proposition must stand on its own: a reader who has not seen the article must be able to understand it. Resolve pronouns, give full names, and include the time, place and population when the claim's truth depends on them. Add nothing else.
3. State the proposition as a claim about the world, not about the article. When an article reports a claim made by a person or a study, state the claim itself and record the source in "relation" and "source"; do not write "the article says".
4. Keep the article's meaning. Do not strengthen, weaken, generalise or soften the claim.
5. Leave out rhetorical flourishes, questions, and claims whose meaning cannot be resolved from the article.
6. Each proposition must come from the article it is listed under. Copy, character for character, the shortest passage of that article that states it ("span"). The passage must be one continuous stretch of the article, with every word, letter and punctuation mark exactly as in the article: do not change a word, do not shorten it with "...", and do not join passages from different places. Copy the passage as it stands even where the proposition itself resolves a pronoun or gives a full name.
7. List every proposition the article contains. Do not list the same proposition twice in different words.

For each proposition, give "relation": "asserts" (the article states it in its own voice), "reports" (the article reports a person, group or study saying it), or "hedges" (the article states it with doubt or qualification), and "source": who makes the claim (a person, group or study as named in the article, or "the article" when it is the article's own voice).

Return JSON of the form {{"articles": [{{"article": "<label>", "propositions": [{{"text": "<proposition>", "span": "<exact passage>", "relation": "asserts|reports|hedges", "source": "<who>"}}, ...]}}, ...]}}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.

template.name: label_A.txt
template.text:
The following news article is labelled {labels}. The name of the outlet has been removed.

{articles}

Task: extract every sentence of the text of the article labelled {target}, in order, and classify each sentence by type and by tone.

Copy each sentence exactly as it appears in its article, character for character. Do not include the headline: in each article, the line after the label and date is the headline, and it is not a sentence of the text. Do not skip any sentence, and do not merge or split sentences. A sentence ends at a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark, or at a closing quotation mark that follows one of these, unless the mark is part of an abbreviation or a number.

If the article is a transcript, in which passages begin with a speaker's name followed by a colon (for example "SMITH:"), leave the speaker's name and the colon out of the sentence, and treat each sentence as said by that speaker.

Decide the type in this order, and use the first that applies:
1. "quote": the sentence's main content is words of a person or source given in quotation marks, or, in a transcript, words said by anyone other than the outlet's own host or reporter. Each sentence of a quotation that runs over several sentences is a quote. A sentence that reports what someone said without quotation marks, outside a transcript, is not a quote; classify it by the rules below.
2. "opinion": the sentence expresses the writer's own view, judgement or evaluation.
3. "borderline": the sentence has the form of a factual statement but also contains the writer's own judging or interpreting words.
4. "fact": the sentence has the form of a factual statement. It need not be true; do not judge whether it is true.
5. "other": none of the above, for example a question or a line addressed to the reader.
In a transcript, sentences said by the outlet's own host or reporter are the writer's own sentences: classify them by rules 2 to 5, and a greeting, a thanks or a question put to a guest is "other".

Tone is how the sentence presents its main subject (the person, group, institution, event or policy the sentence is chiefly about), judged from the sentence itself and not from your own view of that subject:
- "positive": it presents the subject favourably;
- "negative": it presents the subject unfavourably;
- "neutral": it presents the subject neither favourably nor unfavourably.
For a quote, judge how the quoted words present their subject.

Return JSON of the form {{"articles": [{{"article": "<label>", "sentences": [{{"n": 1, "text": "<sentence>", "type": "quote|opinion|borderline|fact|other", "tone": "positive|neutral|negative"}}, ...]}}, ...]}}, with one entry in "articles" for each article you were asked about.

cal.title: Calibration: wording, paraphrase and negation, structure, article effects, size
cal.question: Measurements every later experiment needs, independent of its design.
about: Twenty-four statements per topic, three of each kind, taken from the pooled claims of the generation runs; seven topics.

A: nine wordings of the stance request. B: each statement replaced by a paraphrase or by its negation. C: related pairs under different definitions of a relation (fit or clash, evidence, cause). D: all ten articles, each one left out, and each one alone. E1 and E2: about a hundred statements of one topic, and the 168 statements of the seven topics together. S: one statement per request. P: the update request with neighbours who share the agent’s own state, or with none.
Each module was run with no articles and with all ten articles, where that applies.
Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.5 through the Claude Code command line; Opus on two topics. Claude Code’s own system prompt comes first and the study’s system prompt is appended.

steps.label: A. Nine wordings of the stance request
steps.asks: For each statement, say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on a statement, give null for it.

steps.label: B. Paraphrased and negated statements
steps.asks: For each statement, say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on a statement, give null for it.

steps.label: B. Writing and checking the paraphrases
steps.asks: For each statement below, write two paraphrases that say exactly the same thing in different words, and one negation that states the opposite claim (true exactly when the original is false), written naturally rather than by prefixing 'It is not true that'. Keep names, numbers and dates.

steps.label: C. Definitions of a relation
steps.asks: Think about how these statements relate to one another in your own view. List the pairs of statements that are related: for each, say whether agreeing with one makes it more natural to agree with the other (positive) or to disagree with it (negative), and how strongly, as an integer from -3 (strongly in conflict) to…

steps.label: D. Article effects: all ten, one left out, one alone
steps.asks: For each statement, say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on a statement, give null for it.

steps.label: E1. Every kept claim of one topic
steps.asks: For each statement, say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on a statement, give null for it.

steps.label: E2. The seven topics together
steps.asks: For each statement, say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on a statement, give null for it.

steps.label: S. One statement per request
steps.asks: Say how strongly you agree or disagree with it, as an integer from -10 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree), where 0 means you neither agree nor disagree. If you cannot form a view on it, give null.

steps.label: P. The update request, with no new information
steps.asks: Give your current rating of every statement (an integer from -10 to 10, or null if you cannot form a view) and your current view of how the statements relate, listing related pairs only (weights -3 to 3, never 0; each pair once).

exp9.title: Experiment 9: does the answer come from the model's own record?
exp9.question: A model is given four news articles on immigration enforcement, one per prompt. After each article it returns an updated record of propositions and attitudes, and after the last it is asked to answer a user’s question. The experiment asks whether the answer depends on that record.
about: The same four articles, in the same order, in every run.

Nine set-ups: the record is a network or a written summary; the prompt asks for the model’s own beliefs, or (reader-neutral) for the propositions readers of any background might come to believe and then an attitude toward each; each prompt contains the record and the current article, or all articles so far; links are reasons, or state what fits or clashes; and in D no record is kept.
Main run: Claude Haiku 4.5, nine set-ups, four user questions, five runs each. Prompt tests with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

The edit test: before the answer, the record is changed (a proposition’s attitude flipped, a proposition removed or rewritten as its denial, or the whole record rewritten to point the other way), to see whether the answer follows.
